I was curious about these math routines for some other potential uses, so
created the type-in this weekend via 2000 baud AstroBASIC, including the two
variants of Square Root that Tim notes in the original documentation. The
only change I made to the code was to remove one erroneous character in the
title and REM out the ":RETURN" on line 2, since that is for 300 baud BASIC.
Seeing these approaches toward solving what we now take for granted with
native functions and floating point operations is.well, interesting!

 

*	Original - Uses a faster square root function.
*	Enhanced- Uses a more accurate square root function.
*	Core - I took the core functions and placed them in subroutines for
modularity, see below for details.

 

The organization of line numbers is as follows:

 

*	0-95: Menu Selection Screen
*	100-190: SINE input and calculation (lines 160-190 are used only if
INPUT value is more than 45 degrees)
*	200-250: COSINE input and calculation
*	300-370: ARCTANGENT input and calculation
*	400-460: SQUARE ROOT input and calculation (400-500 for the enhanced
square root method)
*	800-840: End of calculation menu to either perform another
calculation or return to the main menu.

 

The original square root function pads the result with +0.3 with a note in
the comments "corrects +/- .3% difference. But this can lead to erroneous
output (e.g., square root of 64 returns as 8.3). However, I found even the
enhanced formula could likewise be quite a few decimals off when calculating
uneven square roots, and is definitely slower.

 

I ran these operations to compare the results to modern calculations as
summarized below:

 

*	SINE (35 Degrees): Bally =  0.579, Modern = 0.5735764
*	SINE (75 Degrees): Bally = 0.966, Modern = 0.9659258
*	COSINE (50 Degrees): Bally = 0.642, Modern = 0.6427876
*	ARCTANGENT (.457 Ratio): Bally = 24.94, Modern = 24.56040069
*	SQUARE ROOT ORIGINAL (64): Bally = 8.3, Modern = 8.0
*	SQUARE ROOT ENHANCED (64): Bally = 8.0, Modern = 8.0
*	SQUARE ROOT ORIGINAL (45): Bally = 6.4, Modern = 6.71
*	SQUARE ROOT ENHANCED (45): Bally = 6.9, Modern = 6.71

 

The "Core" file:

 

This allows you to call any of the four operations from any program. I
placed SINE at line 1000, COSINE at line 2000, ARCTANGENT at line 3000 and
SQUARE ROOT at line 4000. To use any of them, set the variable "S" to the
value you want to submit, then call GOSUB to the routine you want. "S" will
then have the result for your subsequent use. Be warned that the SINE and
COSINE functions also alter variable "T", ARCTANGENT modifies "T" and "U",
and SQUARE ROOT modifies "A", "B" and "T" so if you use those elsewhere
you'll want to manually save/restore their true values.

 

For example, the line below, combined with the CORE library, will print 579
(SINE of angle 35 = 0.579, times 1000).

 

     5 S=35; GOSUB 1000; PRINT S

 

ORIGINAL DESCRIPTION: This program simply computes the 4 routines: SINE,
COSINE, ARCTANGENT, & SQUARE ROOT. When the program is loaded, press 1
through 4 on the keypad to get the functions. You can check these functions
on a calculator and see how accurate they are. Most of the answers come
within 3-thousanths of a degree of the calculation. If you are programming a
3-dimensional game and using these functions for vectors and angles etc.,
they are more than accurate for your purposes. The SINE function is
contained in the lines 100-190. The COSINE function is contained in lines
200-240. The ARCTANGENT function is in lines 300-360. The SQUARE ROOT
function can be found in line 400-450. The numbers that can be used in the
SINE function are 6-99. The COSINE function can use numbers 0-103. Numbers
for use in the ARCTANGENT function are .001-.999 (NOTE: The decimal point is
already on the screen). SQUARE ROOT uses numbers 2-32767.

 

Matt

Admittedly once I had it done I recognized the severe limitations of these
commands. But was still happy to have it for archival purposes and used the
experience as a continued effort to improve and fix several bugs in my MAME
front-end that is still a work-in-progress. I plan to make a video
demonstrating its progress in the coming weeks and know you will be
impressed by its potential!

The constraints of these SINE/COSINE routines to only around 90 degrees is
inhibitive. I was originally going to explore graphic plotting in
conjunction with the knob control, and potentially make use of it for some
game. That said, I believe there are more effective ways to handle these
routines and in many instances it would be much more efficient to create a
static data table of necessary angles/mappings, like in one of the available
arrays for fast reference.

There is an alternative SINE routine in the Bally Artillery type-in seen in
Creative Computing (Aug. 1982), where C = Elevation.

I also found a note in Arcadian Volume 5 Issue 5 (letter dated Feb. 13,
1983) where someone had put a prize money bucket toward the development of

I intentionally designed the low/hi-res screen SRAM board so no Astrocade 50 pin expansion pins are required to operate it. This frees up this expansion for rear hardware plug-ins like say a  User ROM/RAM board, where the User RAM could be designed for use with both the low and hi-res modes.

With hi-res, you would only have 32KB of directly addressable User RAM at 8000-FFFFH. Actually, 32KB is a lot of memory for one person programming in machine or assembly language.

However, one could design extended User RAM that is indirectly addressable using multiple 32KB banks plus decode the User RAM scheme so the banks are software selectable. In this case, you could load a short ML "bank select" routine at the bottom of screen RAM, where the Z80 stack, variables, flags and such are hidden, to switch a 32KB bank, then re-point the Z80 program counter, so program execution would continue at the newly switched 32KB bank.

Now, for my personal use, I am designing an Astrocade rear plug-in board with the following features:

Software selectable multipager for the hi-res screen RAM (16KB x 8 pages = 128KB)

Software selectable low/hi-res screen map

32KB EEPROM providing two 16KB banks @0000-3FFFH, manually selectable

Four User RAM schemes including ZIF sockets, compatible with a 32KB EEPROM

One of these User RAM schemes will utilize a 32 pin 256KB flash memory type SST39SF020A chip and will be decoded to software select 32KB banks at 8000-FFFFH. I bought 10 of these chips.

Now, it is possible to load hi-res programs in the seven 16KB pages of hi-res screen RAM, leaving one page for the hi-res TV display. You do need the software selectable multipager to do this.

As you know, the more sophisticated a User ROM/RAM board is, the more expensive it will be to purchase.

That is the point of this inquiry, to survey any hi-res Astrocade interest among the enthusiasts. Then, decide what to do with that interest.

Note also that I don't have the expertise to design/create "more modern" high-tech schemes. I am "old school".

A while ago, I spent time researching the possibility of utilizing the SD card technology for saving/loading programs and found zero documentation/videos for someone like me, a newbie, interested in learning how to create a more modern high-tech User RAM scheme.

With over 32KB of memory, you really need a fast means to save and load programs. Sadly, I don't have that expertise either. I'm stuck using a 2000 BAUD audio tape interface or copying User RAM to an EEPROM using a fast ML copy routine.

Let's see if there is any other hi-res interest, to see if creating a PC board is even worth the effort. It might be, just for me.

Thanks for your feedback.

I've done more research on this in the past month. First, there is
additional context in a Bally story from DotEaters, excerpted below.
Essentially, some of the support team at ARI (who developed all ROMs and
software for CyberVision in 1977-1979) split off to form Astrovision after
the demise of CyberVision. The core ARI developers instead moved to
California to work for Atari. Ken Charles mentioned in the Arcadian excerpt
is synonymous with Ken Balthaser, who was one of the core software
development members at ARI. A detailed write-up from Ken is included in Part

While I’m finishing up the ICBM Attack controller that I’ve been working on (waiting on the last of the parts and finalizing the joystick bits, should be done this weekend), I got started on, and have now finished, my Arcade Controller for the Bally Home Library Computer / Bally Professional Arcade / Bally Computer System / Astrocade.  So allow me to present my:

Bally Computer System Edition – VVG Enhanced Controller

YHVy7n.png ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img924/8595/YHVy7n.png )

As the purpose of this project was to create for myself, a full-featured, true arcade type controller for the Bally/Astrocade system, (not a “game-specific” controller like I’m working on for ICBM Attack), I stylized this controller in the general likeness of, and matched the aesthetics of, the original consoles and their hand controllers.  So, like the vintage consoles themselves (expect for the white ones of course), it features woodgrain panels on the front, and on both sides…and has a black top/control surface, with gold accenting.  The console that I personally own, happens to be the Bally Computer System variant, so I included a matching logo from the cartridge storage cover, onto the front face of the controller.

gXOF3S.png ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img924/3223/gXOF3S.png )

3xjH7i.png ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img923/5780/3xjH7i.png )

The upper portion of the controller includes an 8-way Joystick and a Trigger button (for games requiring only these controls), and the lower portion includes a control Knob and a duplicate Trigger button (for games requiring only these controls).  My initial thought regarding this project, was that there were going to be a few games that wouldn’t play well with this controller, as it would be very difficult to manipulate the Joystick with one hand, manipulate the Knob with a second hand, and somehow figure out a way to also manipulate a Trigger button, when necessary, with a third hand…for games like Gunfight and/or Missile (and a couple of others).  One possible solution, would be to use a joystick with a top-fire button, so that my two hands could manipulate all three controls.  But top-fire joysticks are fairly rare, and require an extraordinary mounting depth, due to the 5 th switch being mounted below the joystick.  Personally, with tabletop/laptop arcade controllers like these, I really prefer to fully rest the palms of my hands on the control surface, and only use my finger/thumb tips to manipulate the controls.  But with top-fire joysticks, they really feel/play best, when you completely fist-grab the lever/ball knob, so that your thumb is free to operate the top button.  So, for these reasons, I opted not to install a joystick with a fire button, which I felt would sacrifice ergonomics.

But then, when I was shopping for a potentiometer to use for the Knob control, I found out that there are a few models currently available, with a momentary push-button built into them; very much like the pressing/snapping downward of an analog stick, on a modern control/game pad (like those for Sony/Microsoft/Nintendo consoles).  So I ordered and installed one of these potentiometers with a built-in momentary switch, and topped it with a molded reproduction Atari Tempest knob that I have painted brown, to mimic the look of the knob on the original Hand Controllers.  Then, rather than “assigning” the controller knob a port number, like 1/2/3/4 (like the original Hand Controllers), I added a black text over gold background disc, with the Bally logo, into the recessed top surface of the knob.  Thus by using my left hand on the Joystick, and my right hand on the Knob w/ built-in Trigger button, I can play any game that can be played with an original Hand Controller, with this arcade controller.

gAFRGM.png ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img922/2365/gAFRGM.png )

So there you have it, my take on a full-featured arcade controller for the Bally/Astrocade consoles, and below are the specifications of the control hardware:

** Hammond 14" x 8.25" aluminum sloped top enclosure (braced, reinforced, & weighted)

** iL Eurojoystick2 8-way joystick (Sg - 2-1/16), w/ Cherry microswitches, w/ threaded shaft (short), w/ 32mm black ball knob

** iL PSL-C Super Short Concave pushbuttons, w/ Cherry microswitches (D41X), (2) black

** TT Electronics potentiometer w/ momentary pushbutton, w/ Atari Tempest knob (molded reproduction)

** Rear-mounted cord cleats for cable management, w/ 10’ custom crimped controller cable

** Bally Computer System console inspired, CPO artwork

Enjoy!

It is certainly a scarce machine, but I’ve found enough advertisements and evidence spanning years of time from the era that shows it was indeed available at retail…albeit mostly remained a catalog mail-in product. By July 1980 it was liquidated to only $88 and $1 per cassette (originally $399). I’d venture to guess the 10,000 figure mentioned by former employees was the overall purchase order quantity rather than actual consumer sales. Extra stock may have been discarded. Joe Miller (co-founder) mentioned they received a second order batch for the 3001.

 

Chem-Con also retailed the 3001 variant in local Pennsylvania outlets in December 1980 as an attempted reboot after Montgomery Ward severed ties to it. The Chem-Con CEO was asked about the CyberVision in 1983 and said sales “diminished quite a bit” but that they built them to order, so did not have problems with overstock. Unrelated, but years later he and other staffers wound up in a heap of legal trouble and prison over fraud, tax evasion and racketeering when the company collapsed. 

 

In my cross-research with Bally I found an old classified buried in the Bob Fabris collection, possibly from an Arcadian newsletter, where one seller was looking to trade 15 CyberVision data tapes for other system software. One seller on eBay recently sold a few of these systems, though I’m unsure of their origins and none of them included original retail box packaging but did include the manuals. Overall the controller plays great, but I'm probably going to adjust the potentiometer resistance value for the Knob control.  The pots in the stock Hand Controllers are 50k Ohm, but the pot I bought (with the momentary push-button), wasn't available in 50k Ohm, so I bought the 100k Ohm version...knowing I could install a fixed resistor in parallel, and lower the value.  Once I got the pot, taking a measurement of it's max resistance it read, 86k Ohms, which with a +/- 20% tolerance is "technically" within spec.  So by adding a 120k Ohm resistor in parallel with the pot, I now had an operational range up to 50k Ohm, matching that of the original Hand Controllers.  But even though the resistance range is the same, it doesn't play quite the same...and this is something that I had already considered when I was designing the controller.  The knob I'm using has a larger diameter than the Hand Controller knob, (~1.25" vs. ~0.75"), which means it has a larger circumference, and thus my thumb/finger has to travel in a longer arc, to achieve the same "on-screen" action/result when operated.  So it's like the Knob control is desensitized compared to the original (to verbalize this phenomenon), but again, I had already anticipated this.  I did the math this afternoon, and if I simply remove the 120K Ohm resistor I added, the length of the arc with my larger knob, will be mathematically the same as the Hand Controllers, so I'll start there and see how it plays...and adjust further if necessary.

I was playing Space Fortress on level 9 the other night...and it was a heck of a lot easier with the arcade controller then it was with the Hand Controller...especially with the arcade pushbutton, vs the trigger on the Hand Controller.

For me I am most definitely right handed.  I personally grew up with a 2600 and CX-40 joysticks.  Whenever I use a "handheld joystick" (Atari/ColecoVision/Intellivision), I always hold the controller in my left hand, and manipulate the joystick/disc with my right hand.  But, whenever I play with a mounted, or tabletop, or laptop...arcade stick, I almost always manipulate the joystick with my left hand, as my right hand is better with the buttons.  But then, in my formidable years, my buddy and I spent a lot of time one summer playing a Galaga cocktail table at our local Pizza Hut, and the cocktail control panel doesn't have the ambidextrous controls that the upright does...so that's where I think it started for me.  I absolutely can (and sometimes do) play arcade games with my right hand, especially ones that don't need buttons like Pac-Man and similar, but my preference for sure, again with a larger arcade type controller, is joystick left, buttons right.

I'm familiar with Ed's controllers.  He and and I have talked before, and I even used his ColecoVision membrane keypad kits, for a run of ColecoVision controllers that I built a few years ago.  The aluminum sloped top enclosures I use for most of my controllers these days (including these Astrocade versions), are the same (or similar, depending on his current source) that he uses for his.  The biggest difference, is that I wasn't happy with the overall feel of the Hammond enclosures when assembled with only the 4 factory fasteners, so I've added (2) 3/4" leg x 1/8" thick, steel angle braces (and 8 more fasteners) to mine, which really increases their overall rigidity, and adds a nice little bit of weight for stability.  But professionally, I'm in an industrial equipment field, and I always overbuild everything.

As I do all the work for my controllers, (artwork design and printing and laminating, and physical layout design and CNC programming and machining), I don't have to pay premiums to outside designers / vendors / machinists for new and different and one-off designs...so I like building special controllers that are different from one another, and it doesn't affect my cost too much.  I have, and occasionally do sell controllers that are duplicates of ones that I've built before, but unlike some of the other joystick / arcade stick builders that sell on Facebook, Etsy, and/or Ebay, I don't have much interest in mass producing small and inexpensive controllers that anybody can afford.  I'd rather build the bigger and fancier ones that everybody wants, but maybe only a few can afford.  So maybe its that mindset, that is the reason that I'd be excited to build a special controller for Crazy Climber for the Astrocade.  The 2600 had a contemporary port of Crazy Climber...which uses only 1 joystick...wrong!  The ColecoVision has a modern port-"ish" of Crazy Climber, wherein you can use either 1 joystick...wrong, or 2 joysticks, but only using up motions, not having to press each stick up and down...wrong.  So, as the Astrocade seems to have the only port on a contemporary console with a proper control scheme...it seems like a no brainer that it is deserving of a special controller.  The only thing I need to decide on, is what joysticks to use for it.  The arcade originals are incredibly/impossibly rare, so they're pretty much out of the question.  I think my best alternative will be (2) vintage Coin Controls / Happ 8-way joysticks, as they, like the Crazy Climber originals, have a square restrictor built into the housing and use microswitches.  I'll just need to modify their shafts to cut off their molded knobs, and create threads so that I can screw on white resin ball knobs...matching the originals as close as possible.

When I did the original Spectre ICBM handle, I matched the 50K value on the joystick so it would work the same as the Bally handle. And it was hard finding an inexpensive 50k joystick at the time.

20055:
I did some testing with a spare pot and resistor I had.  I measured the full range value of the pot, then manually set it to ~25% of this value, recorded that value, then installed the resistor in parallel both across pins 1 & 3, and 1 & 2, and recorded these values.  I repeated this at the 50% and 75% potentiometer range values.  The linearity stays pretty straight, within ~10%, but the "center" shifts a lit bit of course...which doesn't matter with a non-centering control.  So I did disconnect the additional resistor that I had added to lower the pot down to 50K, and now it plays a lot closer to the Hand Controllers.  Obviously due to the larger vs. smaller knob, it will never feel exactly the same, but it moves the paddle in Brickyard back and forth across the screen a lot faster (with less rotation) than it did, more akin to what I'm use to with the 2600 paddles.

A couple of years ago I created a paddle controller for the Atari 5200, for Kaboom (and a couple other games).  A few others have done a similar project, and some said to use a 500K pot, and some say to use a 1M pot.  The potentiometers in the actual 5200 joystick controllers are ~1.6M Ohm, but due to how the internal potentiometers are manipulated by the external joystick (with some sliding plastic bits), you can only actually realize about 550K of resistance when fully operated.  So for that project, I bought a dual gang 1M ohm potentiometer, and added a switch that would allow me to switch it back and forth from ~500k to a ~1M mode.  While it worked with both values of course, it required a lot more rotation when in 500k mode to move the buckets back and forth in Kaboom, vs. when in 1M mode.  For the first two levels this was ok, but on level 3 and after, it really had to be in 1M mode.  500k mode did work pretty well for Pole Position though.

Pin 1 - Not Connected (not used)
Pin 2 - Down (not used)
Pin 3 - Left (Left Base button N.O. switch contact)
Pin 4 - Right (Right Base button N.O. switch contact)
Pin 5 - Trigger (Middle Base button N.O. switch contact)
Pin 6 - Up (not used)
Pin 7 - Horizontal Potentiometer
Pin 8 - Direction/Trigger Common (parallel (or daisy-chained) to common switch contact of all 3 Base buttons)
Pin 9 - Horizontal Potentiometer

Port 2 Cable:

Pin 1 - Not Connected (not used)
Pin 2 - Down (not used)
Pin 3 - Left (not used)
Pin 4 - Right (not used)
Pin 5 - Trigger (not used)
Pin 6 - Up (not used)
Pin 7 - Vertical Potentiometer
Pin 8 - Direction/Trigger Common (not used)
Pin 9 - Vertical Potentiometer

To add the additional compatibility for Bally Pin, you'd want to add 2 more side-mounted buttons for flipper control, and a ball launch button wired as follows:

Port 1 Cable:

Pin 5 - Trigger (Left Flipper button N.O. switch contact)
Pin 8 - Direction/Trigger Common (to common switch contact of Left Flipper button)

Port 2 Cable:

Pin 5 - Trigger (Right flipper button N.O. switch contact)
Pin 6 - Up (Ball Launch button N.O. switch contact...technically can be any of the 4 directional contacts...I chose Up)
Pin 8 - Direction/Trigger Common (to common switch contact of Right Flipper and Ball Launch buttons)

Under no circumstances should a site like this deduct money from the customer before it gets acknowledgement that the label has been successfully generated and available to print by the user. Many years ago this is how USPS used to operate their website and it caused me all kinds of grief. You’d get charged instantly to print a label, but half the time their buggy system wouldn’t actually generate the label or it’d appear in some Java applet half corrupted and you were then out the money and still had no usable label. My mission here, was to finish my Bally/Astrocade arcade controller trilogy, so allow me to present my newest masterpiece:

Crazy Climber Edition - VVG Enhanced Controller

ITmsXZ.png ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img924/4439/ITmsXZ.png )

Its probably pretty safe to say that nobody has ever built a twin-stick arcade controller for the Astrocade before.  But as the Crazy Climber port on this contemporary console is the only one which features a proper arcade control scheme, I felt I needed to build this.  Artistically I opted to replicate the Nichibutsu upright arcade cabinet control panel, versus the more common, and more plain, Taito silk-screened aluminum control panel.  Due to my controller enclosure only being 17" wide, versus the original cabinet being ~24" wide, I had to crop and modify the artwork/controls slightly.  An original example is below:

xBcMED.jpg ( https://imagizer.imageshack.com/img924/3711/xBcMED.jpg )

The central character artwork remains full sized, and the center-to-center distance between the joysticks remains an arcade accurate 8".  But as I didn't have the same overall width of the arcade control panel, I did have to make a few small changes.  First, the Astrocade port doesn't need P1 and P2 start buttons like the arcade original.  But it does need Knob and Trigger controls for the console menu's game selection, and the in game control scheme selection.  So rather than install these to the left of the "Left" joystick in a vertical column (like the original P1/P2 start buttons), which may interfere with my left hand when playing, I installed them in a horizontal row, centered above joysticks.  So the upper left control is the Knob control labeled as "Select" and the upper right control is the Trigger control labeled as "Start."  I opted for a knob and a pushbutton that had black outer edges with a red center, to mimic the look of the original "Single/Double" start pushbuttons.  I then shrunk the large instruction card to the right of the "Right" joystick, and placed 1 of these smaller versions on each side of the main artwork, for symmetry.  Then for the joysticks, as the arcade originals are near impossible to find, I selected a model that could closely mimic the look and feel of the originals, as much as possible.  For these, I chose vintage late 80s Happ joysticks which I have modified.  Originally these were bat lever joysticks, so I cut off the bat tops, and threaded the shafts to accept threaded ball knobs.  Then I installed lightweight springs and custom designed actuators, which loosen the overall feel, and allow for much more responsive actuations, which also shortens the overall throws.  These are microswitch joysticks that also feature square physical restriction like the originals, and I even cut square joystick clearance holes in the panel, to mimic those on the original panel.  Here are the details:

** Hammond 17" x 11.50" aluminum sloped top enclosure (braced, reinforced, & weighted)

** (2) Happ 8-way joysticks, w/ Cherry microswitches, w/ lightweight springs, w/ threaded shafts, w/ GGG Hand Candy midnight slate ball knobs

** Bourns potentiometer, w/ black/red knob

** NKK LP01 pushbutton, black/red

** Rear-mounted cord cleats for cable management, w/ twin 10’ custom crimped controller cables, w/ port ID labels

I also find it odd, but I suppose that was a conscious, if misguided,
corporate decision to separate arcade from home as much as possible.
Interestingly, Atari did the same thing in the 70s for the VCS, including
with their launch titles: Air-Sea Battle, Basic Math, Blackjack, Combat,
Indy 500, Star Ship, Street Racer, Surround, and Video Olympics. Outside of
Basic Math and Blackjack (if I recall correctly) all of those had Atari
arcade equivalents/origins, but you'd never know from most of the names
(which were changed) or how they were marketed (certainly nothing
associating them with the arcade). That would more or less continue until
the release of the first real blockbusters, Asteroids and Space Invaders,
although even then there was no specific branding of "The arcade experience
at home" for the most part. It really wasn't until the ColecoVision that a
company went hard on the arcade association on the console side of things,
and it clearly worked at the time, although, to be fair, the arcade
market/pop culture presence was much bigger by 1982 than it was in the 70s.
By that time, most of the major companies were going hard with identifying
with popular arcade properties, though of course the Astrocade's window of
relevancy in that regard had long since passed for a variety of reasons.

There are so many things we all would have done differently in hindsight if
we worked at these companies, and I think changing up the packaging and
marketing is certainly in the top 10. All of these companies were finding
their way, breaking new ground, and they certainly all had plenty of
missteps that seem obvious in hindsight.

I've always assumed that when Bally sold the console to Astrovision (later renamed Astrocade, obviously), the deal didn't include the rights to the titles of the arcade conversions. The reason could be that CBS already had the cartridge rights for their upcoming 2600 releases, but this doesn't explain why Astrocade was able to issue the games themselves without alteration, regardless of what they called them.

I can't think of any reason why the guys at Astrocade would deliberately decrease potential sales by changing the names, unless it was indeed a rights conflict. And unless I'm forgetting one, -all- of the arcade titles were changed, at least outside the built-in ROM. A cartridge even came out with the name Space Invaders on it, before that was replaced. So it's not as if they didn't see the importance of recognition.

But as you've indicated, maybe it was just a decision that's easy to see as misguided in hindsight.


>
I also find it odd, but I suppose that was a conscious, if misguided, corporate decision to separate arcade from home as much as possible. Interestingly, Atari did the same thing in the 70s for the VCS, including with their launch titles: Air-Sea Battle, Basic Math, Blackjack, Combat, Indy 500, Star Ship, Street Racer, Surround, and Video Olympics. Outside of Basic Math and Blackjack (if I recall correctly) all of those had Atari arcade equivalents/origins, but you'd never know from most of the names (which were changed) or how they were marketed (certainly nothing associating them with the arcade). That would more or less continue until the release of the first real blockbusters, Asteroids and Space Invaders, although even then there was no specific branding of "The arcade experience at home" for the most part. It really wasn't until the ColecoVision that a company went hard on the arcade association on the console side of things, and it clearly worked at the time, although, to be fair, the arcade market/pop culture presence was much bigger by 1982 than it was in the 70s. By that time, most of the major companies were going hard with identifying with popular arcade properties, though of course the Astrocade's window of relevancy in that regard had long since passed for a variety of reasons.

There are so many things we all would have done differently in hindsight if we worked at these companies, and I think changing up the packaging and marketing is certainly in the top 10. All of these companies were finding their way, breaking new ground, and they certainly all had plenty of missteps that seem obvious in hindsight.

All of the enclosures I use are factory manufactured (ABS, or aluminum, or steel) enclosures, or formerly "retail sold arcade sticks" (like for the Sega Saturn or the Sony Playstation, or similar) that I repurpose.  I'm using a 17" x 11.5" sloped-top, powdered coated, aluminum enclosure from Hammond (1456RL1BKBK) for this Space Fortress controller, similar to the Mouse Trap example above, but that was the wider 20" version...as I needed more room.  This 17" enclosure costs about $55, plus tax, plus shipping.  These enclosures are 2 pieces of bent aluminum, with the bottom piece, making up the bottom and the 2 sides, and the top piece making up the control surface and the front and the back, with two narrow "bottom" faces on the top half, which is how/where the two halves are fastened for assembly:

This picture, here above, is of a 14" enclosure machined previously for the Galaxian (Midway Cocktail) controller pictured below, featuring authentic arcade original controls, and a few extra bits specifically for the ColecoVision) :

I do take issue with the overall feel of these enclosures when "factory" assembled with only 4 screws on enclosures </= 14", and 6 screws on enclosures >/= 17. So you can see the 2 steel angle braces at the bottom of the picture above (unassembled enclosure), that I cut & install below the control surface, 1 on each side, where they meet the upright sides.  This prevents the upright sides from winging outward (exposing gaps), prevents downward bowing of the control surface from the weight of your hands, and adds a nice little bit of extra weight so it won't move around when playing. Plus it then basically "connects" all of the sides of the enclosure, so that it feels like a "solid" box...versus feeling like 2 separate halves, kind of fastened together.

I have a CNC mill at work that allows me to machine the control surface, but all of the enclosure modifications for assembly and bracing have to be done by hand...laying out holes, pilot drilling holes, finish drilling holes, tapping holes, and countersinking holes (as necessary)...for 2 extra assembly screws on the 14" enclosures and increasing the factory #6 assembly screws to #8 assembly screws on all enclosures, for the screw mounted rubber feet on the bottom (vs. adhesive feet), for the installation of the steel braces, for installing the rear mounted cord cleats, and for installing the rear cord grip.  I usually have about 1.5 - 2.5 hours of "machining" time (CNC and hand-work) for each of these.  Then another 1 to 2 hours for assembly, and another 1 to 2 hours for wiring...depending on how much wiring there is.

Its a labor of love!

As a 46 year old man (born in 1976)...I have been playing video games most of my life, and I grew up during the heydays of the arcades...and thus I love arcade games, especially ones I have fond memories of.  Sure we had ports of arcade games on our home consoles/computers, but obviously they were never as good as their arcade counterparts, mostly because a $40 - $50 cartridge, being played on a $200 - $300 console, could never compete with the hardware of a dedicated, 1 game, $2000 arcade cabinet.  As I would love to fill my house with arcade cabinets...they simply cost too much, are too damn big, and with the ones I'd want now being over 40 years old, are subject to break-downs, and thus needing repairs.  So building these larger Enhanced and Experience controllers like I do, is my way to bring part of the arcade experience home...in a way that takes up a lot less space, and is a lot less expensive, comparatively.  A lot of these types of controllers that I build, are built due to the arcade game having some sort of unique controller, or control scheme...that while yes it can be played with a console's stock controller...that's not how it was meant to be played.  And since arcade cabinets almost always had lots of beautiful artwork, I always try to replicate as much of it as I can, as faithfully as I can.  With that said, my newest controller features probably the least amount of artwork of any of the controllers I've built, but that's how the arcade cabinet was, so without further ado, introducing my:

Space Fortress (Space Zap) - VVG Enhanced Controller

While I couldn't source the original arcade buttons, the Suzo HAPP Large Round buttons are very close in size to the originals, and with my modifications to them (changed out the microswitches for leaf switches, and shortened the plunger springs), they feel very similar to the originals.  Artwork-wise...what little there is of it, I took cues from the full-size upright and cabaret arcade cabinets, as well as details from the Bally/Astrocade port of Space Fortress itself.  Then, I did find out when researching the game, that there were a few other "ports" of similar games on other consoles including Cosmic Ark for the 2600, so I made myself a short Bally/Astrocade to 2600 adapter cable, which re-pins the Aim and Fire buttons (joystick and button controls) from the Bally/Astrocade pinout to the Atari pinout...so that this controller can also be used on other consoles, for other games, when & where appropriate.  Its definitely a lot different playing Space Fortress with a controller like this versus the Hand Controllers, or even my arcade stick controller...and it is very satisfying, to feverishly slap the large buttons during gameplay.  And finally, for complete Bally/Astrocade console compatibility, I installed a Knob and redundant Trigger control, where the P1 & P2 start buttons were on the original arcade cabinets (marked as Select and Start).  This way, the menu, and game selections, can all be made directly from the controller itself, versus having to use the console's keypad for these options.

I'll admit, if someone told me a couple of months ago that there would be 4 unique controllers worthy of being built for the Bally/Astrocade, I would have told them they were crazy...but here we are...#4.  Enjoy!

As there is no arcade version of Cosmic Raiders, there is "technically," no "wrong way" to create/design CPO graphics for a Cosmic Raiders arcade controller.  But personally, I do try to adhere to the styling & concept precedents, set forth by most of the arcade games from the past, with these 3 general rules when I'm creating new artwork:

The game's name, in large fancy stylized artwork, is for the marquee...not the CPO.  That's not to say the name of the game cannot appear on the CPO, but not super large and taking up the entire panel.

Beautiful graphical artwork (like the box or manual cover art from a home console game), is for the side-art...not the CPO.  Again, that's not to say some artwork cannot appear on the CPO, but not 1 large picture that fills the entire surface, wherein the installed joystick and buttons diminish the overall look of the art.

A screenshot of the game would be displayed on the monitor...and thus no reason to duplicate it on the CPO.

So what that leaves then, and what "normally" appears on a CPO is simple and usually geometric art: some arrows/pointers around the joystick indicating what directions it can be moved in, some text near/under/over the installed controls describing the functions of each of the controls, maybe some text boxes providing some gameplay hints/tips (although sometimes these cards are on the monitor bezel), and in the case of Galaga, a couple of tiny "screen-shots" detailing how to let a ship get captured, then re-claimed for double firepower.

As always...not hard and fast rules that must be adhered to...but this is how most old-school arcade games were, and what I try to mimic.

Back to your speed evaluation. Both Bally and Astro BASICs use the byte swap with the video RAM. This means that each and every WORD needs to be split into 2 and half goes to the BASIC and the other half goes to the screen.Blue Ram BASIC does NOT split the WORDs. It is WYSIWYG. It enters all of the BASIC text directly to memory. It does NOT share the video RAM. Which actually quadruples the execution speed of some program areas.However there are a few slow-up commands. The "IF" statemen is the worst. It has to do "Evaluate Expression" several times during it's process. Then there are the GOSUB and GOTO commands. How they work is when a GO... is executed, it must go to the first byte of the program and check every byte looking for the exact line number match. It see a line number. If it doesn't match, it goes to the end of the line (one byte at a time) and then see the "GO" at the end and it then looks at the next line number for a match. If the line number is near the end on the program, it will have to go thru it all to find it.
I hope this helps when you are designing you next program.To help with the "IF" statements, try to use a mathematical equation. I.E.
55 if TR(1)=0goto 5556........
55 goto 55+TR(1)
It also saves 3 bytes of space in the program.

Back to your speed evaluation. Both Bally and Astro BASICs use the byte swap with the video RAM. This means that each and every WORD needs to be split into 2 and half goes to the BASIC and the other half goes to the screen.
Blue Ram BASIC does NOT split the WORDs. It is WYSIWYG. It enters all of the BASIC text directly to memory. It does NOT share the video RAM. Which actually quadruples the execution speed of some program areas.
However there are a few slow-up commands. The "IF" statemen is the worst. It has to do "Evaluate Expression" several times during it's process. Then there are the GOSUB and GOTO commands.
How they work is when a GO... is executed, it must go to the first byte of the program and check every byte looking for the exact line number match. It see a line number. If it doesn't match, it goes to the end of the line (one byte at a time) and then see the "GO" at the end and it then looks at the next line number for a match. If the line number is near the end on the program, it will have to go thru it all to find it.

I hope this helps when you are designing you next program.
To help with the "IF" statements, try to use a mathematical equation. I.E.

55 if TR(1)=0goto 55
56........

55 goto 55+TR(1)

It also saves 3 bytes of space in the program.

“Astrovision had gotten its start a few years previous during the genesis year of the mass-produced personal computer; in 1977, as a company called Authorship Resource Inc. (ARI). The core development team of ARI then drifted away, with others such as general manager Martin S. Albert and salesman Ray George forming Astrovision from the ashes. In 1981 the company, led by president Martin Albert, relaunches the old Professional Arcade as the Bally Computer System.”

So there is definitely a connection. The business description for Astrovision was: “Manufacturer and sale of electronic video games and home computers, manufacturer and sale of consumer electronic products and any, and/or all lawful acts of or business as permitted by the laws of the State of Ohio.” You can see Martin Albert’s signature as the president of Astrovision, dated August 4, 1980. The original 1978 release of Bally BASIC used an external 300-BAUD audio interface, which you can see here:

https://ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/audio_interface/audio_interface.html

The 1981 re-release of the Bally BASIC cartridge, referred to as "AstroBASIC," has a 1/8" jack built into the cartridge to accept an audio cable to save and load programs more quickly at 2000-BAUD.  This means that a user has to constantly plug in and unplug cables depending on if a BASIC program is being saved or loaded from a tape.

A popular project was to build a manual switch to avoid this cumbersome method of changing the audio cables. The "Arcadian" published an article about it called "I-O Switch For New Bally BASIC Cartridge" by Steve Walters in the December 1981 issues, here:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_02.pdf#Page=4

When I built this switchbox in 2001, twenty years after the project was published in the newsletter, I was still able to take a trip to my nearest Radio Shack store, at the time it was in Liverpool, New York (a small suburb of Syracuse, NY) and buy the parts using the same part numbers listed in the article.  I still use this switchbox whenever I use AstroBASIC to this day.  Nearly every tape that I have digitally archived has been saved to a WAV file though this neat little project.  This tape I/O box has served me well for two decades!

I created an entire new sub-section of my BallyAlley website to hold these two pictures because I hope that over time other Bally Arcade users who have built a similar tape I/O interface for use with AstroBASIC will send me pictures of it which I'll add to this area of the site.

--------------------

You have accepted a dare (after much prodding of course) to pilot a boat (by using joy stick 1) through the "Black Lagoon", to a dock on the other side.  This lagoon is no ordinary, run of the mill type, lagoon. It can only be navigated by passing through the interconnecting waterways. Any attempt to pass between sections of the lagoon other than by using the connecting waterway will be blocked.

Each waterway has a pump station, which will come in handy, as the boat which you are to attempt this journey with has a very bad leak and cannot be fixed. Upon arrival at a waterway, by checking your bilge level you will be able to determine whether you need to use the pump station. Should you elect to use the pump station press trigger 1. Your score is then reduced and the creature hearing the pumps will surface and come for you. The location which he surfaces will vary, therefore, varying the time it takes him to reach you, this will determine the time you have to pump down. Just before he reaches you, by pushing the joy stick to the right you can enter the next section of the lagoon and temporarily escape the creature. 

The creature is constantly roaming the depths of the lagoon unseen by human eyes. Should you happen to be at the same place he is or if you allow your bilge level to reach "full", causing you to sink, the creature will capture you. The "Black Lagoon", also, has the mysterious capability to change shape and to change the location of the waterways and dock with each new attempt.
